sources.quote: We do you to wit that on the thirteenth day of the month of October you were deposed from the episcopate and made a stranger to all ecclesiastical order

sources.work: Zachariah of Mitylene (Pseudo-Zachariah), Chronicle III.2 (trans. Hamilton and Brooks)
sources.quote: in the monasteries, and severed themselves from his communion.

links.named_in_text: cyrilline-miaphysite-egyptian-tradition longDescription and why (Chalcedon's wording refused, Dioscorus deposed, imperial authority backing the Chalcedonian side)

Timothy Aelurus's own refutation of Chalcedon is vendored (Armenian with German, ter-Mekerttschian 1908) and could document a separate 'argued against' link from the Egyptian side; I did not draft it.

links.note: In 457 Alexandria's anti-Chalcedonian party consulted 'the whole order of the monks' and chose Timothy as bishop. He was an ascetic once brought from the desert to Cyril and ordained by him. A much later Coptic history says the letters of a later patriarch, Peter, were kept at the Monastery of Macarius.

sources.work: Zachariah of Mitylene (Pseudo-Zachariah), Chronicle IV.1 (trans. Hamilton and Brooks)
sources.quote: And they agreed upon Timothy, a man expert in business 5 and of ascetic life ; who had been brought from the wilderness, by force, to Cyril, and ordained as presbyter by him.

sources.work: Zachariah of Mitylene (Pseudo-Zachariah), Chronicle IV.1
sources.quote: they all took courage, and consulted with the whole order of the monks as to whom they should make the bishop of the believing party.

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, Life of Peter (trans. Evetts, PO 1)
sources.quote: All his epistles are preserved in the Monastery of Father Macarius;

links.named_in_text: cyrilline-miaphysite-egyptian-tradition relationsSummary ('Continuation of ... Desert') and legacy ('a monastic life descended unbroken from the desert')
drafter_flags: The first Zachariah quote carries the translator's footnote marker '5' after 'business' and a space before the semicolon, exactly as in the file.

'Gave rise to' claims only that monks of the desert passed into the new church; the note does not say the church came from the desert alone. The Alexandrian see is its other parent, and that see has no census entry (see escalations).
The History of the Patriarchs is a much later compilation; it is used only for the Macarius archive, and the note says it is late.

links.note: Cassian heard Abbot Serapion of Scetis list eight principal faults, ending with pride. Gregory the Great later made pride 'the queen of sins' and set seven principal sins beneath her. Gregory names no source, so the link rests on the likeness of the two lists.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences V.2 (Abbot Serapion, On the Eight Principal Faults)
sources.quote: fourthly anger, fifthly dejection, sixthly acedia, i.e., listlessness or low spirits, seventhly cenodoxia, i.e., boasting or vain glory; and eighthly pride.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Morals on the Book of Job XXXI.87 (trans. Bliss)
sources.quote: when pride, the queen of sins, has fully possessed a conquered heart, she surrenders it immediately to seven principal sins, as if to some of her generals,

drafter_flags: The route ran through Cassian, a Gallic writer; a reviewer may prefer this link from gallic-monastic-ascetic-christianity. I drafted it from the desert because the desert text names Gregory and the list is a Scetis elder's.
Bliss's OCR has 'lo lay it waste' just after the quote; the quote stops before it. Bliss numbers the paragraph 87 within Book XXXI (the chapter is often cited as XXXI.45).

links.note: Eusebius copies a letter from Constantine to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, about building a church at the site of Christ's tomb. The emperor writes that he has no greater care than to adorn that spot with a splendid building.

sources.work: Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.30 (Constantine's letter to Macarius)
sources.quote: that I have no greater care than how I may best adorn with a splendid structure that sacred spot,

links.change_reason: New: the Jerusalem text opens with Constantine's builders and no link carried the imperial church's part.

links.note: Jerome describes Paula, his patron, worshipping at the tomb of the Resurrection in Jerusalem. Yet he told a friend that heaven was as easy to reach from Britain as from Jerusalem.

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 108 (Epitaph of Paula), section 9
sources.quote: and when she entered the tomb which was the scene of the Resurrection she kissed the stone which the angel had rolled away from the door of the sepulchre.

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 58 (To Paulinus), section 3
sources.quote: Access to the courts of heaven is as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem;

drafter_flags: Jerome also wrote against Bishop John of Jerusalem (Against John of Jerusalem, npnf206). That would document an 'argued against' link, but neither text names that quarrel, so I did not draft it.
Group C (hieronymian) may draft the same pair; the merge should reconcile.
links.change_reason: New: the Jerusalem summary sets itself beside Jerome's circle, and no link joined them.

links.note: Jerome says Hilarion, Palestine's first monk, visited Jerusalem for a single day so as not to neglect the holy places. In the 380s the pilgrim Egeria saw monks and virgins come to the tomb church before dawn for the daily office.

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 58 (To Paulinus), section 3
sources.quote: The blessed Hilarion, though a native of and a dweller in Palestine, only set eyes on Jerusalem for a single day, not wishing on the one hand when he was so near to neglect the holy places,

sources.work: Egeria, Pilgrimage 24.1 (trans. McClure and Feltoe)
sources.quote: all the monks and virgins, as they call them here, go thither, and not they alone, but lay people also, both men and women, who desire to begin their vigil early.

links.named_in_text: palestinian-ascetic-monasticism-early longDescription ('Pilgrims passed through all of it ... some of them stayed'); jerusalem-liturgical-pilgrimage-christianity longDescription ('resident clergy and monks')

links.change_reason: New: both texts name pilgrims and resident monks sharing the holy places, and no link carried it.

links.note: Writing at Bethlehem around 390, Jerome made Hilarion of Gaza the subject of a Life. He says Epiphanius of Salamis, who knew Hilarion well, had already praised him in a letter. Jerome presents his book as taking up that work.

sources.work: Jerome, Life of Hilarion, section 1
sources.quote: It is true that that holy man Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, who had much intercourse with Hilarion, set forth his praises in a short but widely circulated letter.

sources.work: Jerome, Life of Hilarion, section 1
sources.quote: And so we in taking up the work begun by him do him service rather than wrong:

links.named_in_text: palestinian-ascetic-monasticism-early longDescription ('Jerome, writing from Bethlehem, gave the movement its literature'), why, legacy
drafter_flags: The date 'around 390' rests on the NPNF editors' chronology (npnf206 line 2988: '390. Lives of Malchus and Hilarion, hermits.'), not on Jerome's own words.
Direction: the later side (Jerome's circle) names and uses the earlier (Hilarion and the letter about him), so the arrow runs from the Palestinian monks.
links.change_reason: New: the Palestinian text names Jerome as its literary voice in three fields and no link carried it.

prose_changes.old: Egyptian in origin - Hilarion was Antony's disciple - and the direct antecedent of chalcedonian-monasticism-judean-desert-and-gaza, which begins where this leaves off at c. 450.
prose_changes.new: Egyptian in origin: Hilarion learned the life from Antony. It is the forerunner of the Chalcedonian monasteries of the Judean desert and Gaza, which begin about 450, where this leaves off.
prose_changes.reason: The sentence printed a raw movement id to readers; the plain name replaces it. 'Direct antecedent' claimed more than the evidence: the link to the Chalcedonian monasteries is Inferential-Thin, resting on place and sequence. 'Forerunner' keeps the order of the two without claiming the same community.

prose_changes.old: Jerome, writing from Bethlehem, gave the movement its literature: a Life of Hilarion, and a Life of Malchus about a monk taken by Saracen raiders.
prose_changes.new: Jerome, writing from Bethlehem, gave the movement its literature in a Life of Hilarion. He also wrote a Life of Malchus, a Syrian monk taken by Saracen raiders.
prose_changes.reason: Malchus was not a Palestinian monk. Jerome places him at Maronia, east of Antioch, and in the desert of Chalcis, and he was taken on the road from Beroea to Edessa (Life of Malchus 2-4, npnf206 lines 31137-31205). The next sentence ('Both are shaped to teach ...') still reads correctly.

prose_changes.old: Jerome told the story of the loneliest of these lives in his Life of Malchus, a monk carried off by raiders.
prose_changes.new: Jerome told the story of a lonelier life still, farther north, in his Life of Malchus, a Syrian monk carried off by raiders.
prose_changes.reason: Same correction as the longDescription: Malchus was a monk of the Syrian desert of Chalcis, not one of the Palestinian lives (Life of Malchus 2-4).

prose_changes.old: Jerome's Life of Hilarion also did something more particular: it established the saint's life as a Latin literary form, on the model of the Life of Antony, and gave the West a second template for it.
prose_changes.new: Jerome's Life of Hilarion also did something more particular. Written about 390, it followed his own Life of Paul and the Latin Life of Antony, and helped make the saint's life a Latin literary form.
prose_changes.reason: The Life of Hilarion did not establish the form. Its own prologue refers back to Jerome's earlier Life of Paul (npnf206 lines 30115-30117); Jerome lists the Life of Paul first among his works (De viris 135, npnf203 line 41790); and Evagrius of Antioch had already put Athanasius's Life of Antony into Latin (De viris 125, npnf203 lines 41678-41682). No vendored text says Jerome modeled Hilarion on the Life of Antony.

prose_changes.old: He died at Kellia in January 399, months before a controversy his own learned circle could not survive — a bishop's letter on how literally to picture God split simple monks from learned ones, and by the year's end Evagrius's circle had been driven out of Egypt.
prose_changes.new: He died at Kellia in January 399, just before a controversy his own learned circle could not survive. A bishop's letter on how literally to picture God split simple monks from learned ones, and soon afterward Evagrius's circle was driven out of Egypt.
prose_changes.reason: Cassian says Theophilus's festal letter reached the desert a few days after Epiphany of that year (Conferences X.2, npnf211 lines 35951-35975), so 'months before' does not fit a January death. Socrates (VI.7) tells the expulsion but gives no year, so 'by the year's end' is replaced with 'soon afterward'. The one long sentence is also split in two.

prose_changes.old: Benedict's own Rule for Western monks sends its readers directly to John Cassian's reports from Egypt, and the monasteries of Sinai and Mount Athos trace their own practice back to the same desert source.
prose_changes.new: Benedict's own Rule for Western monks sends its readers directly to John Cassian's reports from Egypt. In the East, the Philokalia, gathered on Mount Athos and printed in 1782, opens with counsels credited to Antony and carries Evagrius and Cassian too.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text shows the monasteries of Sinai or Athos tracing their own practice to the desert, and the Athonite and Sinai entries do not say so. The vendored Philokalia (1893 edition of the 1782 anthology compiled on Athos) opens with Antony the Great (line 1017) and includes Evagrius (line 58634) and Cassian (line 58646), which shows the later Eastern tradition reading the desert in its own words.

prose_changes.old: Modern dialogue has largely concluded that the fifth-century split was as much about vocabulary as about belief: a series of joint declarations from the 1970s onward record Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic representatives agreeing that they confess the same faith in Christ in different words.
prose_changes.new: Modern dialogue has argued that the fifth-century split was as much about vocabulary as about belief. Joint statements since the 1980s record Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic representatives agreeing that they confess the same faith in Christ in different words. Historians still debate how far that holds for the fifth century itself.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text covers the dialogue. The repo names the 1984 Syriac Orthodox-Catholic common declaration and the 1989-1990 Vienna agreed statements (Build/worlds/wsyr/Step0_Movement_Scope_Confirmation.md), not a 1970s declaration, and its own review judged the 'only words' reading Contested, not Widely Accepted. The new text reports the dialogue's position as its own and says the reading is disputed.

prose_changes.new: Carries on the church of Alexandria and the monks of the Egyptian desert.
prose_changes.reason: Note-style shorthand ('+') replaced with a plain sentence. The meaning is unchanged; the desert half now has a link, and the Alexandrian half names a see with no census entry (see escalations).

prose_changes.old: Comparison-point for the Bethlehem Circle's distinctiveness on record
prose_changes.new: A near neighbor of Jerome's circle at Bethlehem, whose members worshipped at Jerusalem's holy places even as Jerome wrote that heaven was as near from Britain.
prose_changes.reason: The old phrase read as cataloguing commentary ('comparison-point', 'on record'). The new sentence states the relationship the new link documents: Paula at the tomb (Ep. 108.9) and Jerome's 'as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem' (Ep. 58.3).

prose_changes.old: The manuscript disappeared for centuries and was rediscovered in an Italian library in 1884, and it remains the single most valuable eyewitness account of early Christian worship anywhere.
prose_changes.new: The manuscript disappeared for centuries. It was found again at Arezzo, in Italy, in 1883, and it remains the single most valuable eyewitness account of early Christian worship anywhere.
prose_changes.reason: Bernard's edition says the manuscript 'was discovered in 1883 at Arezzo'; Gamurrini announced it in 1884 and published it in 1887 (egeria_pilgrimage-of-silvia_bernard1896.txt lines 7776-7782; McClure and Feltoe, lines 117-119).

prose_changes.old: A western pilgrim named Egeria kept a detailed diary in the early 380s recording exactly what was done and when, a manuscript lost for centuries and rediscovered in an Italian library in 1884.
prose_changes.new: A western pilgrim named Egeria kept a detailed diary in the early 380s recording exactly what was done and when. The manuscript was lost for centuries and found again at Arezzo, in Italy, in 1883.
prose_changes.reason: Same date correction as the longDescription (Bernard 1896: discovered 1883 at Arezzo). The sentence is also split in two.

prose_changes.old: Cyril's lectures remain a primary source for how baptism and communion were explained to newcomers in the fourth century, and Egeria's diary is read wherever early liturgy is studied.
prose_changes.new: The lectures of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, remain a primary source for how baptism and communion were explained to newcomers in the fourth century. Egeria's diary is read wherever early liturgy is studied.
prose_changes.reason: Clarity only: Cyril appears here for the first time in the entry and is easily taken for Cyril of Alexandria. His Catechetical Lectures are vendored (npnf207). The sentence is also split in two.

escalations: Cross-world / portfolio: the census has no entry for the church (see) of Alexandria in the fourth and fifth centuries. Two of my movements name it as parent: Aksum ('Child of Alexandria': Frumentius consecrated by Athanasius) and the Cyrilline tradition ('Continuation of Alexandria'). The only Alexandrian entry, alexandria-catechetical, is the catechetical school, and linking Athanasius's or Cyril's church to it would misstate both relationships. Sources are ready if Mark rules that alexandria-catechetical should stand for the see or adds an entry: Socrates I.19 (npnf202 lines 4356-4358, 'but Frumentius arriving at Alexandria, reported the affair to Athanasius the bishop, who had but recently been invested with that dignity;'), Athanasius, Defence before Constantius 31 (npnf204 lines 36150-36151, 'this Frumentius was advanced to his present rank by Athanasius,'), and Zachariah IV.1 for Cyril and Timothy. I drafted no Alexandria link.

Possible duplicate entries: cyrilline-miaphysite-egyptian-tradition ('from 451', era 2) and cyrilline-miaphysite-egyptian-christianity (451-642, era 3) describe the same church from the same year, and the first's continuesAs points to the second. I drafted a sourced continued-as link so the field has evidence either way; whether to merge them is a portfolio decision.

Rule question, not decided by me: the brief says to qualify a no-entry claim that no vendored or repo-cited source supports. The Aksum text's Ezana sentences (his conversion; coins dropping the disc and crescent for the cross; 'one of the earliest such declarations by any state') are standard numismatic fact but have no such source. Rewriting them to 'may have' would mislead the other way, so I left them and listed the wanted texts. Same for the legacy's twentieth-century patriarch and the Cyrilline entry's 'worshipping increasingly in Coptic rather than Greek'. Mark may rule whether qualify applies to well-established facts that merely lack a vendored source.
